prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A U.N. special investigator called for the resignation of top Kenyan officials and sweeping changes in the country's security forces to end reported widespread killings by police across the African nation. The report urged President Mwai Kibaki to publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending the killings. "The special rapporteur concluded that police in Kenya frequently execute individuals and that a climate of impunity prevails," Philip Alston said in a report a recently submitted to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva. "Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations." The report calls for the resignation of Kenya's attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. It also says Kenyan President Mwai Kibaki should publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending unlawful killings by the police. The Kenyan government expressed its "deep displeasure" with the report, questioning the special investigator's "approach, conduct and method of work." "The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur," said Alfred Mutua, a spokesman for the Kenyan government. "His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya's sovereignty." Alston also accused government security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men in a March 2008 crackdown on a militia in the Mt. Elgon district, in western Kenya. And he said there was compelling evidence that what he called police death squads were operating in Nairobi and Central Province with a mandate to "exterminate" suspected Mungiki gang members. "These are not "rogue" squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors," he said. The Mungiki militia, which is loyal to Kibaki's Kikuyu tribe, began as a religious sect, but over the years has morphed into a gang that runs protection rackets -- particularly in the slums. The U.N. investigator suggested Kibaki acknowledge the alleged police killings and commit to stop them. He also advocated creating an independent civilian police oversight body, and said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should investigate violence after the 2007 election. He urged the government to create a witness protection program as well. Alston, who investigates human-rights problems around the world for the United Nations, traveled to Kenya at the government's invitation. He stayed for 10 days in mid-February while 100 interviews were conducted in the U.N. member nation. There is hope for Kenya despite his criticism, Alston said. "While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable," the report says. "If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings."

(CNN) -- A U.N. special investigator has called for the resignation of senior Kenyan officials and sweeping reforms to the country’s security forces to end reported widespread police killings across the African nation.

The report urged President Mwai Kibaki to publicly affirm his commitment to ending the killings.

“The special rapporteur concluded that police in Kenya frequently execute individuals and that a climate of impunity prevails,” Philip Alston said in a report recently submitted to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva.

“Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations.”

The report calls for the resignation of Kenya’s attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. It also says Kibaki should publicly affirm his commitment to ending unlawful killings by police.

The Kenyan government expressed its “deep displeasure” with the report, questioning the special investigator’s “approach, conduct and method of work.”

“The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur,” said Alfred Mutua, a spokesman for the Kenyan government. “His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya’s sovereignty.”

Alston also accused government security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men during a March 2008 crackdown on a militia in the Mt. Elgon district of western Kenya.

He said there was compelling evidence that what he described as police death squads were operating in Nairobi and Central Province with a mandate to “exterminate” suspected members of the Mungiki gang.

“These are not ‘rogue’ squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors,” he said.

The Mungiki militia, which is loyal to Kibaki’s Kikuyu tribe, began as a religious sect but has evolved over the years into a gang that runs protection rackets, particularly in the slums.

The U.N. investigator recommended that Kibaki acknowledge the alleged police killings and commit to ending them. He also advocated the establishment of an independent civilian police oversight body and said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should investigate the violence that followed the 2007 election. He further urged the government to create a witness protection program.

Alston, who investigates human rights problems around the world for the United Nations, traveled to Kenya at the government’s invitation. He spent 10 days there in mid-February, during which 100 interviews were conducted in the U.N. member nation.

Despite his criticism, Alston said there is hope for Kenya.

“While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable,” the report says. “If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings.”
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A United Nations investigator has urged senior Kenyan officials to step down and called for broad reform of the nation’s security services in response to reports of extensive police killings.

In a report recently delivered to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva, Philip Alston said Kenyan police routinely carry out executions while facing little or no accountability. He described as particularly alarming the presence of police death squads that allegedly take orders from high-ranking officers to kill suspected leaders and members of criminal groups.

The report recommends that Kenya’s attorney general resign and that the police commissioner be replaced immediately. It also calls on President Mwai Kibaki to publicly recognize the unlawful killings attributed to police and pledge to bring them to an end.

Kenya’s government reacted with “deep displeasure,” challenging the special investigator’s methods, behavior and overall approach.

Government spokesman Alfred Mutua said authorities were gravely concerned by the accusations in Alston’s report. He added that Alston’s criticism of the foundations of the Kenyan state—especially its institutions—was entirely unacceptable and infringed upon the country’s sovereignty.

Alston further alleged that Kenyan security forces tortured and killed hundreds of men during a March 2008 operation against a militia in the Mt. Elgon district of western Kenya. He also said persuasive evidence showed that police death squads were active in Nairobi and Central Province under instructions to “exterminate” people suspected of belonging to the Mungiki gang.

According to Alston, these units were not made up of rogue officers acting independently; rather, they were police personnel following direct commands from their superiors.

The Mungiki militia is aligned with Kibaki’s Kikuyu tribe. Although it originated as a religious sect, it gradually developed into a criminal gang involved in protection rackets, particularly in impoverished urban neighborhoods.

Among his recommendations, Alston proposed establishing an independent, civilian-led agency to oversee the police. He also said the International Criminal Court’s prosecutor should examine the violence that followed Kenya’s 2007 election and urged the government to set up a witness protection program.

Alston, whose U.N. role involves examining human rights concerns worldwide, visited Kenya at the government’s invitation. He spent 10 days in the U.N. member country in mid-February, during which 100 interviews were conducted.

Despite his harsh assessment, Alston said Kenya’s problems could still be addressed. The report stated that, although conditions were serious, they were not impossible to resolve and that Kenya could substantially reduce unlawful killings if its leaders chose to act.

outputs.L4:
A United Nations special investigator called on Kenya’s government to confront allegations that security forces had carried out widespread extrajudicial killings and systematic torture. Following an inquiry into the conduct of police and other security agencies, the investigator urged senior officials implicated in the failures to resign and recommended sweeping reforms to ensure that officers could be held accountable.

The report said there was compelling evidence that police death squads had detained, tortured, and executed suspects, often disposing of their bodies without proper investigation. These actions were not described as isolated misconduct by rogue officers, but as part of an organized and recurring practice carried out with the knowledge or authorization of senior commanders. Victims reportedly included suspected criminals and members of outlawed groups, as well as people targeted during security operations.

According to the investigator, Kenya’s justice system had repeatedly failed to respond to the abuses. Police rarely conducted credible inquiries into deaths involving their own personnel, while prosecutors and other officials did not take effective action even when substantial evidence was available. Witnesses, human-rights defenders, and victims’ relatives faced intimidation, further limiting the possibility of accountability.

The report concluded that these failures had created a pervasive culture of impunity in which security officers could torture or kill with little fear of prosecution. It called for independent investigations, stronger civilian oversight of the police, protection for witnesses and activists, and institutional reforms aimed at preventing political interference and command-level cover-ups.

The investigator also urged President Mwai Kibaki to make an unequivocal public commitment to ending extrajudicial executions and to ensure that those responsible—including senior officials—were investigated and prosecuted. Such a statement, the report argued, was necessary to demonstrate that the abuses were not tolerated at the highest levels of government.

Kenyan authorities rejected the findings, disputing the credibility of the allegations and insisting that the government did not sanction unlawful killings. The investigator, however, maintained that the evidence was consistent and extensive, and that official denials could not substitute for transparent investigations. The report warned that without meaningful accountability and comprehensive police reform, the pattern of torture, executions, and institutional protection for perpetrators was likely to continue.

I can’t reproduce CNN’s exact house style, but here’s a concise, attribution-heavy breaking-news article in a mainstream cable-news format.

---

## U.N. investigator alleges widespread police killings in Kenya, urges top officials to resign

**NAIROBI, Kenya** — A United Nations investigator has accused Kenyan police of carrying out widespread extrajudicial killings and called for the country’s police chief and attorney general to resign over what he described as a systemic failure to investigate and prosecute those responsible.

Philip Alston, the U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, said police death squads were allegedly operating with impunity, targeting suspected criminals and members of the outlawed Mungiki sect.

His report described the killings as organized and systematic rather than the work of a few rogue officers. It also alleged that authorities routinely failed to conduct credible investigations, allowing police officers accused of abuses to escape accountability.

Alston called for the resignation of Police Commissioner Hussein Ali and Attorney General Amos Wako, arguing that both had failed to address longstanding allegations of unlawful killings.

Kenyan officials rejected the report’s conclusions, accusing the investigator of relying on unverified testimony and failing to recognize the security threats facing the country. Police have previously denied operating death squads and maintained that officers use lethal force only when necessary.

Human rights organizations have documented bodies found in forests, fields and morgues, some bearing gunshot wounds or signs of torture. Activists say many victims had been detained or last seen in police custody.

The allegations come amid broader concerns about Kenya’s justice system following the violence that erupted after the disputed 2007 presidential election. More than 1,000 people were killed and hundreds of thousands displaced during the unrest.

Alston warned that persistent impunity could further undermine public confidence in Kenya’s institutions. He urged the government to establish an independent police oversight body, protect witnesses and ensure that allegations against security officers are investigated by authorities outside the police chain of command.

The U.N. investigator’s findings do not carry the force of law, but they are likely to intensify domestic and international pressure on Kenya’s government to reform its police and justice institutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news report on the U.N. Human Rights Council investigation into alleged police executions in Kenya under President Mwai Kibaki.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. inquiry accuses Kenyan police of systematic executions under Kibaki**

**GENEVA/NAIROBI, June 2009** — A United Nations investigation has accused Kenyan police of carrying out widespread extrajudicial killings and operating with near-total impunity under President Mwai Kibaki, while senior officials failed to investigate or prosecute those responsible.

Philip Alston, the U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, told the U.N. Human Rights Council that Kenyan security forces had been implicated in the execution of suspected criminals, members of the outlawed Mungiki sect and people detained during counterinsurgency operations in the Mount Elgon region.

Alston’s findings followed an official visit to Kenya from Feb. 16 to 25, 2009, during which he met government officials, police representatives, civil-society groups, witnesses and relatives of victims. His report concluded that unlawful police killings were not isolated acts by a handful of rogue officers but part of a broader pattern sustained by weak oversight and an unwillingness to hold security personnel accountable.

“The police in Kenya frequently execute individuals,” Alston said in presenting his conclusions. He argued that the absence of credible investigations had created a system in which officers could kill suspects with little fear of arrest or prosecution.

### Allegations involving Mungiki suspects

A central part of the inquiry concerned the killing and disappearance of suspected members of Mungiki, a banned movement with roots among the Kikuyu community. The group had been linked to extortion, organized crime and brutal attacks, particularly in Nairobi, Central Province and parts of the Rift Valley.

Kenyan human-rights organizations alleged that police responded with an undeclared campaign of executions. Bodies of young men were found in forests, fields and mortuaries, often with gunshot wounds. In other cases, witnesses said men were arrested or taken away by officers and were never seen alive again.

The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, then the country’s statutory rights body, documented hundreds of alleged killings and disappearances associated with the security crackdown. Alston said the evidence he reviewed supported claims that police death squads had targeted suspected Mungiki members rather than arresting and prosecuting them through the courts.

The government maintained that police were confronting an exceptionally violent criminal organization and denied that there was an official policy of execution. Officials also disputed the scale and reliability of the allegations.

### Mount Elgon operation examined

The U.N. inquiry also investigated abuses in the Mount Elgon district of western Kenya, where security forces fought the Sabaot Land Defence Force, or SLDF, an armed militia accused of murder, torture, forced recruitment and the displacement of civilians.

The government deployed the military and police to the area in 2008. While the operation weakened the militia and restored a measure of security, witnesses and rights organizations reported torture, arbitrary detention, disappearances and unlawful killings by state forces.

Alston said the crimes committed by the SLDF did not excuse abuses by the security services. He criticized the government for failing to establish what had happened to detainees and for not conducting independent investigations into deaths linked to the operation.

### Senior officials criticized

The report placed responsibility not only on individual police officers but also on senior officials and institutions. Alston sharply criticized Attorney-General Amos Wako, saying his office had repeatedly failed to prosecute security personnel despite extensive evidence of unlawful killings.

He called for Wako’s resignation, describing the attorney-general as a central symbol of Kenya’s culture of impunity. Wako rejected the criticism and said his office could act only when investigators submitted sufficient evidence.

The report also faulted the police leadership and called for an independent civilian body with the authority and resources to investigate police misconduct. At the time, complaints against officers were generally handled within the police force, an arrangement rights groups said allowed evidence to be concealed and investigations to stall.

Alston urged Kibaki’s government to publicly acknowledge the scale of extrajudicial killings, dismiss officials who obstructed accountability and undertake far-reaching reform of the police, prosecutorial system and forensic services.

### Government rejects findings

Kenyan authorities strongly rejected the U.N. conclusions. Government representatives described the report as one-sided, sensational and overly reliant on claims from activists and non-governmental organizations.

Officials said Alston had ignored the danger posed by criminal gangs and armed militias and had exceeded his mandate by calling for the removal of senior officeholders. They insisted that Kenya had functioning courts and investigative bodies capable of addressing criminal allegations.

The dispute became part of a broader confrontation between the Kibaki administration and international critics following Kenya’s 2007 election crisis. More than 1,000 people were killed and hundreds of thousands displaced in the violence that followed the disputed presidential vote. Kibaki remained president under a power-sharing agreement with Prime Minister Raila Odinga, but promised police, judicial and constitutional reforms moved slowly.

### Killings of rights activists heighten concern

The U.N. investigation took on added urgency after the March 2009 killing of two Kenyan human-rights activists, Oscar Kamau Kingara and John Paul Oulu. Both had worked on or discussed allegations of police executions.

Kingara was shot dead in Nairobi by gunmen shortly before he was due to meet Alston’s team, according to rights groups. Oulu was later shot near his home. Kenyan authorities denied state involvement, but the killings intensified fears among witnesses and campaigners and reinforced demands for independent investigations.

Alston said threats against human-rights defenders and witnesses were part of the wider accountability crisis. He warned that people who supplied information about police abuses faced intimidation and potentially lethal retaliation.

### Council role and recommended reforms

The inquiry was conducted through the Human Rights Council’s system of independent special rapporteurs rather than by a tribunal with power to prosecute. Alston could gather evidence, issue findings and recommend reforms, but the United Nations could not directly bring criminal charges against Kenyan officers or officials.

His recommendations included:

- creating a genuinely independent police-oversight authority;
- establishing an autonomous and professional office of public prosecutions;
- strengthening witness protection;
- improving forensic and post-mortem procedures;
- opening credible investigations into alleged police death squads;
- prosecuting officers and commanders where evidence justified charges; and
- reforming police recruitment, discipline and command structures.

The report added international weight to claims Kenyan rights organizations had raised for years: that police were sometimes used as executioners rather than law-enforcement officers and that institutional failures protected those responsible.

Although the Kibaki government rejected the characterization of the killings as systematic, the U.N. inquiry increased pressure for reforms that later included changes to the Constitution, prosecution services and civilian police oversight. For families of the missing and dead, however, the central demand remained unresolved: independent investigations capable of identifying perpetrators and bringing them before a court.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the allegations made by U.N. special rapporteur Philip Alston against Kenya’s security forces, particularly regarding the Mt. Elgon crackdown and suspected Mungiki members.
counterfactuals.output:
In a 2009 report following a visit to Kenya, U.N. Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions Philip Alston alleged that Kenyan security forces had engaged in widespread, organized unlawful killings and that the government had failed to investigate or prosecute those responsible.

- **Mt. Elgon crackdown:** During the 2008 joint military-police operation against the Sabaot Land Defence Force, Alston said security personnel indiscriminately detained local men, systematically tortured suspects and caused deaths and disappearances. He alleged that some detainees were executed or died from abuse, while bodies were concealed or families were denied information. Although he acknowledged the SLDF’s serious atrocities, he argued that these did not justify collective punishment, torture or extrajudicial killing.

- **Suspected Mungiki members:** Alston said there was credible evidence that police death squads had deliberately executed alleged members of the Mungiki sect, particularly during the 2007 crackdown. Suspects were allegedly arrested or abducted, shot—often execution-style—and their bodies left in forests, roadsides or mortuaries. He described the killings as systematic and apparently authorized or tolerated by senior police officials, rather than isolated misconduct.

Alston also accused Kenyan authorities of denying the abuses, intimidating witnesses and human-rights defenders, and failing to conduct independent investigations. The Kenyan government and security agencies rejected many of his conclusions, saying the operations targeted violent criminal and militia groups and disputing claims of an official execution policy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an international news story covering calls to replace Kenya’s police commissioner and attorney general, establish civilian police oversight and witness protection, and investigate post-2007-election violence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Calls grow for Kenyan police chief, attorney general to be replaced**

**NAIROBI, Kenya —** Kenyan authorities faced renewed calls to replace Police Commissioner Hussein Ali and Attorney General Amos Wako, create independent civilian oversight of the police and strengthen witness protection as pressure mounted for accountability over violence following the disputed 2007 presidential election.

Human rights advocates said senior officials should be removed to restore public confidence and ensure credible investigations into killings, sexual violence and other abuses committed during the crisis. They also urged the government to investigate allegations that police used excessive and, in some cases, lethal force against demonstrators.

The post-election violence erupted after President Mwai Kibaki was declared the winner of the December 2007 vote over opposition leader Raila Odinga. About 1,300 people were killed and hundreds of thousands driven from their homes before a power-sharing agreement ended the unrest in early 2008.

Calls for reform include establishing an independent civilian body with authority to investigate complaints against police officers and refer cases for prosecution. Activists say existing internal disciplinary mechanisms lack independence and have failed to hold officers accountable.

They also warned that witnesses to politically organized attacks and alleged police shootings could face intimidation or retaliation without a properly funded and independent protection program. Weak safeguards, they said, could undermine prosecutions and discourage survivors from testifying.

A commission led by Justice Philip Waki documented abuses by police and armed groups and recommended prosecutions of those most responsible. It also called for the creation of a special tribunal, warning that evidence could be handed to the International Criminal Court if Kenya failed to act.

The government has pledged reforms, but critics say progress has been slow and that continued delays risk entrenching impunity. Police and government officials have previously defended the security response as necessary to contain widespread unrest, while saying allegations of misconduct should be investigated.

International partners have urged Kenya to implement the commission’s recommendations, protect witnesses and establish credible accountability mechanisms. Rights groups say replacing senior justice and security officials would be an important first step, but must be accompanied by independent investigations and prosecutions regardless of rank or political affiliation.
